title: The Tulaneans and the lost banjo on the train to Mobile
summary: Hirsch recalls the Tulaneans jazz band at the Strand, then his work with Leslie George at the Battle House in Mobile when he left Leslie's guitar and banjo on the train.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: I didn't know his son. How about the Tulaneans? The Tulaneans? Yeah. Well that was a group of guys from the Tulane band. Right. But it was a jazz band. It was a jazz band. We played at the Strand Theater for a week. Uh huh. We had a dancer, a cheerleader dancer, something like that. We were on the stage there for a week. I'll never forget it was the week that we played LSU. What year are we talking about? I left in 27. Must have been in 27. Strand Theater. Yes. Who was in the band? You got me naming so damn many things now my brain is clamming up. But I can tell you from the pictures who their names were. They went out on a trip. Some guy was booking them. I'm out of town. I didn't go with them because I mean I was working with a local band. I was working with Leslie George and his Society Music. You ever heard Leslie George? Leslie George. We were playing over at the Battle House on New Year's Eve. I'll tell you. The Barrel House? Huh? You said the Barrel House? Battle House. Battle House. It's a hotel in Mobile. And we went over during the day because Dave Winston, uh, Dave Jacobson, the fiddle player, Harry Burke, he couldn't get over there during the day. And Leslie couldn't get over during the day. They were all working during the day and they were going to catch a train and get over there at 9 o'clock that night. So Leslie gave me his guitar and his banjo to take with me. And when they got on the train we put them on the racks of the day coach. And we had all the drums, instruments, and all the, uh, in the, on the, back of the train, on the train there right now, where you get off the thing. So when we get to Mobile, the guys are bugging me. I need money for this. Who we gonna meet when, what time we gonna be this? Okay. So we got that straight and we got the instruments off and we had to meet somebody that was gonna take us where we were supposed to go. We forgot and left the guitar and the banjo on the train. And they were both good instruments. Oh boy. So about 5 o'clock that afternoon, Jake Ginsberg, Jake, Jimmy Gable, Jake Ginsberg was playing trumpet with us. I said, let's go set up the band. He said, that way we can have dinner and we won't be in grand rush or anything like that. So I went down to the ballroom. And we started looking for Leslie's guitar and band. Couldn't find it. What the hell? Somebody playing a joke, hiding it. So we went up in the room, we looked under the bed, we looked in the closet and we looked under everything that we had. Couldn't find it. I was starting to realize, I think we must have left it on the train. Well, in those days you didn't have the telephone services and, you know, computer services and like that that you got today. And the first stop was Montgomery, which wouldn't be until about 6 o'clock that evening. And we had, we went down to the trains to find out if we could find out if they knew anything about it and so forth and so on. No way we could find out. So we came back to, there was a fellow by the name of Ed Benton who was a trombone player with him. His father used to be a violin maker, Ed Benton, used to be on Elks Place. And we called Ed and said, look, you know somebody over here. And on New Year's Eve, everything over there closes up. Wow. It's like a Mardi Gras deal. And everything closes up. So we finally got the, Ed got a hold of this guy that had a music store over there. Yes, I'm sorry.

So we got, we got Ed Benton. And he gets over there and he gets, he gets a banjo. And if you ever saw an old black Joe banjo, this was an old black Joe banjo. No resonator on the back of it. No, I mean it was a, like if you took a broom and put a, put a string down the thing like that. So we put it on Leslie's chair. And when we, when he got there we were already playing the tune. And he picked up the banjo and he started playing. He says, it's very funny, very funny. He said, now where's my instrument? I said, we got a surprise. We can't talk to you now. Wait until after we finish playing this number. And boy, he blew his stack of some of the fears. He says, here I get tickets, birth tickets for you all to go to sleep. Cause we were leaving around two o'clock in the morning. To go to sleep and you wouldn't have to stay up all night. And this is the appreciation I get for that. There's his brother out there. He can't open the door like that. No, he can't open the door. Let him sit there. So, that was the story. Well, we finally, we finally located the, finally located the banjo and the guitar and we got him back. Well, that went all the way to New York. Wow. Cause that was on that train that went to New York.
